r: Every recursive resolver keeps copies of the answers it receives. Each record has a TTL, a 32-bit counter of seconds defined in RFC 1035, which lets the resolver reuse the answer without asking the authoritative server again. Suppose you change an A record at noon and its TTL is 3600 seconds. A resolver that was queried at 11:59 will keep giving out the old IP until almost 1 p.m., and clients will trust it because nothing marks it as stale. So the cache expiry window, not your edit, decides how fast the change spreads. Negative answers are cached too. Under RFC 2308, a resolver that cached NXDOMAIN before your new subdomain existed will keep denying it until the SOA minimum runs out. Browsers and OS stub resolvers add their own caches, and some ignore TTLs entirely. This is TTL debt. Operators should drop TTLs to 300 seconds one full old-TTL period before a migration, or the internet will keep following an outdated map.
